title: Bronchiectasis: Confirm the Pattern, Then Prevent the Next Exacerbation
bottomLine: Bronchiectasis is chronic abnormal airway dilation with recurrent infection/inflammation. Confirm structural disease with appropriate chest CT, identify treatable causes and microbiology, optimize airway clearance, and distinguish a routine exacerbation from hemoptysis or respiratory failure requiring urgent care.
recognize: Chronic productive cough, recurrent lower-respiratory infections, persistent sputum and intermittent hemoptysis are common clues.
Consider bronchiectasis when repeated 'pneumonias' recur in similar regions or symptoms persist between infections.
differentiate: COPD and asthma can coexist, but bronchiectasis requires structural airway disease rather than symptoms alone.
Cystic fibrosis, immune deficiency, aspiration, prior severe infection and nontuberculous mycobacterial disease can be causes or associations.
assessment: Characterize sputum burden, exacerbation frequency, hemoptysis, dyspnea, oxygenation, smoking/exposure history, aspiration risk and prior organisms.
Review vaccination, airway-clearance technique and medications that may worsen secretion retention.
workup: Use high-resolution chest CT when structural confirmation is required and obtain sputum microbiology during clinically important exacerbations or when chronic infection is suspected.
Investigate underlying causes when presentation, age or severity suggests a specific disorder rather than labelling disease idiopathic prematurely.
management: Teach individualized airway-clearance therapy and treat exacerbations using severity, prior microbiology and local antimicrobial guidance.
Refer to respiratory care for recurrent exacerbations, chronic Pseudomonas or other difficult organisms, significant hemoptysis, declining lung function or uncertain cause.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe repeated empiric antibiotics without considering prior cultures, resistance and whether the episode is truly an exacerbation.
Long-term macrolide or inhaled-antibiotic strategies require specialist-guided indication and adverse-effect/resistance monitoring.
counselling: Teach airway clearance, hydration as appropriate, vaccination, smoking avoidance and when sputum/hemoptysis changes require reassessment.
followUp: Track exacerbations, symptoms, microbiology and lung function rather than judging control from one visit.
examTrap: Treating every productive-cough flare with the same antibiotic without reviewing prior organisms or asking whether bronchiectasis has an underlying treatable cause.
oneLinePearl: In bronchiectasis, the next infection matters—but so do airway clearance, prior cultures and the reason the airways became damaged.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society bronchiectasis clinical resources

title: Pulmonary Hypertension: Recognize Right-Heart Strain and Refer by Cause
bottomLine: Pulmonary hypertension is a hemodynamic syndrome with multiple causes, not one medication diagnosis. Suspect it from unexplained exertional dyspnea, syncope or right-heart findings, use echocardiography to estimate probability, search for common cardiac/pulmonary/thromboembolic causes, and refer suspected pulmonary arterial or chronic thromboembolic disease for definitive hemodynamic classification.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pressure, presyncope/syncope, edema and signs of right-ventricular strain are concerning.
Symptoms can be nonspecific; a normal lung examination does not exclude important pulmonary vascular disease.
differentiate: Left-heart disease, chronic lung/hypoxic disease, chronic thromboembolic disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension require different management.
Echocardiography estimates probability and cardiac effects; right-heart catheterization is required for definitive hemodynamic classification when indicated.
assessment: Assess functional limitation, syncope, volume status, oxygenation, thromboembolic history, connective-tissue disease, liver disease, drugs/toxins and left-heart/lung disease clues.
workup: Obtain ECG, chest imaging, echocardiography and cause-directed pulmonary/cardiac testing; evaluate chronic thromboembolic disease when clinically plausible.
Do not start disease-specific pulmonary vasodilator therapy solely from an elevated estimated pulmonary pressure on echocardiography.
management: Treat contributing hypoxemia, volume overload and underlying heart/lung/thromboembolic disease while arranging specialist assessment for suspected precapillary pulmonary hypertension.
Pregnancy or decompensated right-heart failure requires urgent specialty management.
medicationSafety: Pulmonary arterial hypertension drugs can be ineffective or harmful in the wrong hemodynamic group; classification precedes disease-specific therapy.
Review pregnancy risk and drug-specific contraception/monitoring requirements for teratogenic therapies.
counselling: Explain that 'high lung pressure' has several causes and often needs specialist testing before targeted medication is safe.
followUp: Track functional status, right-heart findings and the underlying disease; escalating symptoms require earlier reassessment.
examTrap: Starting a pulmonary arterial hypertension drug because an echocardiogram estimates high pulmonary pressure without establishing the hemodynamic cause.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary hypertension is a syndrome; classify the cause before targeting the pulmonary vessels.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society pulmonary hypertension resources

title: Sarcoidosis: Prove the Pattern and Check the Organs That Change Risk
bottomLine: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous diagnosis made from a compatible presentation, exclusion of important mimics and tissue confirmation when needed. Not every radiographic case requires systemic steroids; cardiac, neurologic, ocular and severe pulmonary involvement change urgency.
recognize: Bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, pulmonary symptoms, erythema nodosum, uveitis or other multisystem findings can suggest sarcoidosis.
Constitutional symptoms are nonspecific and infection, malignancy and other granulomatous disorders remain in the differential.
differentiate: Tuberculosis, fungal disease, lymphoma and occupational/environmental granulomatous disease can mimic sarcoidosis.
Asymptomatic/stable pulmonary disease is different from organ-threatening cardiac, neurologic, ocular or progressive pulmonary disease.
assessment: Ask about dyspnea/cough, visual symptoms, palpitations/syncope, neurologic symptoms, skin/joint findings, calcium-related symptoms and infectious/exposure risks.
workup: Use chest imaging, pulmonary function and organ-directed evaluation; obtain tissue from the safest high-yield site when confirmation is needed.
Do not use serum ACE as a stand-alone diagnostic test.
management: Observe selected stable disease with structured follow-up; use systemic anti-inflammatory/immunomodulatory treatment when symptoms, progression or organ risk justify it and involve specialists for high-risk organs.
medicationSafety: Before prolonged corticosteroid/immunosuppressive therapy, assess infection risk, vaccination, bone/metabolic risk and monitoring requirements.
counselling: Explain that sarcoidosis can involve organs beyond the lungs and that treatment intensity depends on organ risk, not the chest image alone.
followUp: Monitor symptoms, pulmonary function and organ-specific findings according to disease phenotype and treatment.
examTrap: Diagnosing sarcoidosis from hilar adenopathy or an ACE level alone without excluding infection/malignancy—or treating every stable case with systemic steroids.
oneLinePearl: Sarcoidosis is a pattern plus exclusion; organ threat decides urgency and treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory practice resources

title: Adult Cystic Fibrosis: Coordinate Airway, Nutrition, Infection, and Modulator Care
bottomLine: Adult cystic fibrosis is complex multisystem care. The NP should recognize pulmonary exacerbation and complications, support airway clearance/nutrition/adherence, screen for CF-related diabetes and other extrapulmonary disease, and coordinate CF-centre care including genotype-appropriate modulator therapy.
recognize: Increasing cough/sputum, dyspnea, fatigue, weight loss or lung-function decline can signal pulmonary exacerbation.
Pancreatic insufficiency, malnutrition, sinus disease, CF-related diabetes, liver disease and fertility/reproductive issues are common care domains.
differentiate: A CF pulmonary exacerbation is not managed like uncomplicated community bronchitis; prior airway microbiology and individualized CF plans matter.
CF-related diabetes has disease-specific screening/management considerations and should not be treated as ordinary type 2 diabetes by default.
assessment: Review respiratory symptoms, airway-clearance adherence, prior organisms, weight/nutrition, GI symptoms, glucose history, liver disease, bone health, mental health and reproductive goals.
workup: Use CF-centre protocols for sputum microbiology, lung function, nutrition and complication screening; genotype and prior treatment determine modulator eligibility.
management: Coordinate airway clearance, inhaled therapies, antibiotics for exacerbations based on prior microbiology, pancreatic/nutrition support and genotype-appropriate CFTR modulator therapy through specialty care.
medicationSafety: CFTR modulators and chronic antimicrobial regimens have drug-interaction and organ-monitoring requirements; verify current product monographs and CF-centre guidance.
Do not interrupt chronic CF therapies casually during an acute illness without reviewing the individualized plan.
counselling: Reinforce airway-clearance routines, nutrition, infection-prevention practices, fertility/pregnancy planning and early contact with the CF team for exacerbation symptoms.
followUp: Ongoing multidisciplinary CF-centre follow-up is standard; primary care should close preventive-care gaps without fragmenting specialty management.
examTrap: Treating an adult with CF and worsening sputum as ordinary acute bronchitis without reviewing prior organisms, lung-function trajectory and the CF-centre plan.
oneLinePearl: Adult CF is airway disease plus multisystem disease; prior microbiology and the specialty plan drive acute decisions.
sourceBasis: Health Canada CFTR modulator product monographs

title: Mechanical Ventilation: Treat Oxygenation and Ventilation Without Creating New Injury
bottomLine: When an intubated patient deteriorates, assess the patient and circuit before chasing numbers. Separate oxygenation from ventilation, use lung-protective principles when indicated, identify reversible causes of sudden deterioration, and reassess gas exchange/hemodynamics after every major ventilator change.
recognize: FiO2/PEEP primarily influence oxygenation; minute ventilation influences CO2 clearance.
High airway pressures can reflect resistance, reduced compliance, patient-ventilator dyssynchrony or equipment problems.
differentiate: Peak pressure elevation with stable plateau suggests increased resistance; both peak and plateau rising suggests reduced compliance when measured appropriately.
Sudden hypoxemia/hypotension after intubation requires immediate consideration of displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax and equipment failure in addition to disease progression.
assessment: Check airway position, chest movement, breath sounds, SpO2, capnography, hemodynamics, sedation/dyssynchrony, secretions and the ventilator/circuit.
workup: Use ABG/VBG as appropriate, chest imaging and bedside evaluation to answer specific gas-exchange or mechanical questions; trend response rather than ordering gases reflexively.
management: Correct immediately reversible airway/circuit problems, support oxygenation/ventilation, and use lung-protective ventilation for ARDS or other appropriate syndromes with critical-care collaboration.
Weaning readiness requires improvement in the underlying process plus adequate oxygenation, ventilation, hemodynamics and ability to protect the airway.
medicationSafety: Sedation, analgesia and neuromuscular blockade can worsen hypotension/delirium and obscure examination; use protocolized targets and reassessment.
Do not treat ventilator dyssynchrony automatically by deepening sedation before checking pain, airway obstruction, settings and disease physiology.
counselling: When appropriate, explain goals of ventilation, sedation, daily reassessment and liberation planning to patients/families.
followUp: Reassess after ventilator, sedation or airway interventions and document the physiologic response.
examTrap: Responding to sudden desaturation by increasing FiO2 only while missing a displaced tube, mucus obstruction or tension pneumothorax.
oneLinePearl: A crashing ventilated patient is a bedside airway/circuit problem until proven otherwise.
sourceBasis: Canadian Critical Care Society practice resources

title: Asthma and COPD Features Together: Preserve ICS When Asthma Is Present
